t: Cycle Length Queries in a Tree
o: In a complete binary tree labeled heap-style (children of v are 2v, 2v+1), adding edge (a,b) creates exactly one cycle: the path a→root→b plus the new edge. Its length = depth(a) + depth(b) − 2·depth(LCA(a,b)) + 1. Since labels encode paths in binary, finding the LCA is just repeatedly dividing the deeper node by 2 until labels meet — no preprocessing needed. Example 1: LCA(5,3)=1, depths 2 and 1 → 2+1−2+1 = 4 ✓; LCA(4,7)=1 → 2+2−2+1 = 5 ✓; LCA(2,3)=1 → 1+1−2+1 = 3 ✓.
k: Cycle length = dist(a, b) in the tree + 1 = depth(a)+depth(b)−2·depth(LCA)+1.
Heap labeling means LCA = meet point when halving the larger label repeatedly.
Each query is O(log n) with n ≤ 30 — trivially fast even for 1e5 queries.

a.i: Precompute depth of every node (depth[v] = bit_length(v) − 1) and lift nodes level by level to find the LCA, then apply the distance formula.
s: depth(v) = number of bits of v minus 1.
Bring both nodes to equal depth by halving the deeper one.
Halve both until equal — that's the LCA; answer = da + db − 2·dlca + 1.
a.t: O(m log n) — each query climbs at most n levels

a.i: No need to track depths explicitly: repeatedly halve whichever node is larger until the labels coincide, counting steps. Steps = tree distance, so the cycle length is steps + 1.
s: While a ≠ b: halve the larger; count++.
a.t: O(m log n) — at most ~30 halvings per query

w: The simultaneous-climb trick is the cleanest solution — heap labels make parent(v) = v>>1, so LCA computation collapses to a few shifts. Pitfall: use 64-bit/BigInt-safe arithmetic conceptually (labels up to 2^30 fit in int, but shifting habits matter). Edge case: a or b equal to root (cycle through node 1). Follow-up: answer queries on a tree given only parent pointers (then real LCA machinery is needed).
